newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Shenzhen B shares end lower ahead of IPO.
newsitem.headline: Shenzhen B shares end lower ahead of IPO.

text.p: Shenzhen's B share index ended lower on Monday with investors awaiting the B share debut on Tuesday of Wafangdian 2706.SZ, analysts said.
The B index lost 1.31 points or 0.8 percent to close at 162.94 points. Turnover was HK$76.8 million against last Friday's HK81.5 million.
"Wafangdian has good prospects ... it did not lift the B index today because investors want to know see it debuts on Tuesday," an analyst with China Guotai Securities said.
Bearing-maker Wafangdian will list 130 million B shares on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
Wafangdian's B shares are expected to rise 10 percent on Tuesday to HK$3 each from its issue price of HK$2.66, analysts said.
"Investors are encouraged by the price at which SKF bought Wafangdian shares," an analyst at Central-South Securities said.

Swedish Aktiebolaget SKF SKFR.O has bought 65 million B shares at HK$3.575 each or 35 percent above the public offering price in order to enter China's bearings market, lead domestic underwriter China Southern Securities has said.
"The Swedish company paid HK$3.575, so investors believe the shares can rise to that level," a researcher at Sun Hung Kai Investment Services Ltd said.
Uncertainty in the company reporting season also weighed on investors minds.
"Annual reports are still one big factor. What can investors do if companies still haven't published their results?" an analyst at China Guotai Securities said.
Only two out of the 43 B share companies listed in Shenzhen have made their 1996 results public, with the April 30 deadline approaching.
Beverage-maker Shenzhen Shenbao Industrial Co Ltd was the worst performer, losing HK$0.27 or 4.54 percent to HK$5.68 on volume of 146,720 shares.
The A share index gained 11.22 points or 2.61 percent to end at 440.86 points on heavy turnover of 14.5 billion yuan, compared with Friday's 8.73 billion yuan.
More than 10 A share stocks ended the day at their 10 percent limit-up, encouraged by optimism over Shenzhen Development Bank's 1996 result and its dividend plan.
